551.quote_or_event: “Those who act like tyrants are accepted and approved - recognize that this is the sign of the Dark Age of Kali Yuga.”
551.explanation: Guru Nanak lists the marks of a degenerate age, and one of them is that oppression by the powerful comes to be treated as lawful and normal.
551.tie_back: The Kural calls the ruler who habitually harasses his people crueller than a professional killer; Guru Nanak likewise refuses to let accepted tyranny pass as legitimate and names it a sign of moral darkness.
551.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 902, Raag Raamkalee, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
551._accuracy_note: Next-best: the verse condemns tyranny and its acceptance, but it does not compare the tyrant with a murderer or speak specifically of a king's treatment of his subjects.

552.quote_or_event: “Bringing the marriage party of sin, Babar has invaded from Kaabul, demanding our land as his wedding gift, O Lalo.”
552.explanation: Addressing his disciple Bhai Lalo, Guru Nanak describes Babar's invasion as a sinful wedding party that seizes by force what it pretends to receive as a gift.
552.tie_back: The Kural likens a sceptred king's demand for money to a highwayman with a spear saying ‘Hand it over’; Guru Nanak likewise exposes armed power that takes wealth by force under a respectable name.
552.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 722, Raag Tilang (Babarvani), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
552._accuracy_note: Strong thematic fit on extortion backed by force, though the target is a foreign invader rather than a native king taxing his own people.

553.explanation: Guru Nanak condemns the man who sits in the seat of judgment but takes bribes and so denies people what is rightfully theirs.
553.tie_back: The Kural warns that a king who does not examine wrongs and render justice every day loses a little of his country each day; Guru Nanak points to the same failure at the seat of justice.
553.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 951, Raag Raamkalee (Raamkalee ki Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
553._accuracy_note: Next-best: the verse attacks corrupt judges, not a king's neglect, and says nothing of the country's gradual decline.

554.quote_or_event: “Where are the games, the stables, the horses? Where are the drums and the bugles?”
554.explanation: Lamenting the sack of Saidpur by Babar's army, Guru Nanak asks where all the splendour of the ruling class has gone; in the same hymn he says that those who had remembered the Lord beforehand would not have been punished.
554.tie_back: The Kural says a king who bends justice without thought loses wealth and people at once; Guru Nanak pictures a whole order's wealth and pomp vanishing in a single stroke.
554.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 417, Raag Aasaa (Babarvani), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
554._accuracy_note: Next-best: the sudden loss of everything matches, but Guru Nanak traces it to heedlessness of God rather than specifically to the bending of justice.

555.quote_or_event: “But if a powerful tiger attacks a flock of sheep and kills them, then its master must answer for it.”
555.explanation: In his Babar hymns Guru Nanak cries out over the slaughter of the defenceless and insists that the suffering of the weak calls the one responsible for them to account.
555.tie_back: The Kural says the tears of those who can no longer bear their suffering wear away the tyrant's wealth; Guru Nanak likewise makes the cry of the oppressed a demand that power must answer.
555.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 360, Raag Aasaa (Babarvani), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
555._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: the cry of the weak is central to both, but Guru Nanak addresses God as Master of the flock rather than predicting the tyrant's own ruin.

556.quote_or_event: “They alone find peace, and they are the true kings, whose dealings are true.”
556.explanation: Guru Arjan defines true kingship not by power or display but by truthful dealing.
556.tie_back: The Kural says only just rule makes a king's glory endure; Guru Arjan likewise grants the title of true king only to those whose dealings are true.
556.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 962, Raag Raamkalee (Raamkalee ki Vaar), Guru Arjan (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
556._accuracy_note: Next-best: Gurbani's ‘true kings’ are those who trade in the true Name, a spiritual sovereignty rather than the literal ruler whose fame the Kural discusses.

557.quote_or_event: “When it rains, there is happiness. Water is the key to all life.”
557.explanation: Guru Nanak celebrates rain as the source of joy and the sustainer of every living thing.
557.tie_back: The Kural compares a king's lack of kindness to drought on the world; Guru Nanak's verse shows how completely all life hangs on the rain, which is what gives the Kural's comparison its force.
557.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 150, Raag Maajh (Maajh ki Vaar), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
557._accuracy_note: Next-best only: the rain-and-life image matches, but Guru Nanak makes no comparison with a ruler's kindness.

558.quote_or_event: “Their wealth and youthful beauty, which gave them so much pleasure, have now become their enemies.”
558.explanation: Describing the households of Saidpur when Babar's soldiers fell on them, Guru Nanak says the very wealth and beauty they had enjoyed now turned against them.
558.tie_back: The Kural says that under an unjust sceptre having wealth brings more misery than having nothing; Guru Nanak shows exactly this, wealth becoming the owner's enemy under lawless power.
558.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 417, Raag Aasaa (Babarvani), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
558._accuracy_note: Strong fit on wealth becoming a curse under violent rule, though the oppressor here is an invading army rather than the victims' own king.

559.quote_or_event: “Food and wealth are produced in abundance when it rains, if it is the Will of God.”
559.explanation: Guru Amar Das teaches that rain and the plenty it brings come by the divine Will (hukam).
559.tie_back: The Kural says the seasons fail and rain is withheld when a king rules against justice; Gurbani also links rain to a higher order, but places that order in God's Will rather than in the ruler's conduct.
559.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1282, Raag Malaar (Malaar ki Vaar), Guru Amar Das (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
559._accuracy_note: Next-best only: Gurbani makes no causal link between a king's injustice and failing rain; only the idea that rainfall depends on a moral-cosmic order is shared.

560.quote_or_event: “They tax the cows and the Brahmins, but the cow-dung they apply to their kitchen will not save them.”
560.explanation: Guru Nanak rebukes the officials of his day who levied taxes on cows and Brahmins while still clinging to outward rituals of purity.
560.tie_back: The Kural says that when the guardian fails to protect, the cows yield less and the learned forget their scriptures; Guru Nanak also connects the plight of cows and learned men with failing custodians, though his concern is their hypocrisy rather than the loss of Vedic learning.
560.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 471, Raag Aasaa (Asa di Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
560._accuracy_note: Next-best: the pairing of cows and Brahmins under bad rule is striking, but Sikhism rejects the Brahmin's ritual privilege that the Kural's ‘six duties’ presuppose, and the verse mocks ritual rather than lamenting forgotten texts.
